title: Thank them directly
hook: a gratitude letter read aloud gave one of the biggest short-term lifts in early studies

segments.voice: Yesterday: counting blessings, five from the week. Your line was count them.

Somewhere in your past is a person who changed your life and was never properly thanked. A teacher who saw something in you. A neighbor who drove you to the hospital. A coach, an aunt, a friend who stayed on the phone until 3am. It's easy to tell other people about someone like that. Telling them is another matter. For two days the thanks stayed inside you, on a list. Today it goes somewhere.
screen: `THE TEACHER WHO SAW YOU.` → `NEVER PROPERLY THANKED.` → `TODAY IT GOES SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: In the same 2005 study that tested three good things, Martin Seligman's team tried another exercise, the gratitude visit. You write a letter to someone who was especially kind to you but was never properly thanked. Then you deliver it in person and, if you can, read it aloud to them. Of all the exercises in that study, this one gave the biggest boost in happiness in the short run, a clear jump right after the visit. The lift held for about a month, then faded: a single gratitude visit is a big wave, not a new tide. A later study, by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, found something else. Asked to predict how the person would feel getting their letter, the writers guessed too low. They expected it to be awkward, or not to matter much. The people receiving the letters were more pleased, and less awkward, than the writers predicted. The researchers suggest this misjudgment may keep people from saying thanks at all. So the research adds a push to do it on purpose, in words, with some detail. Not thanks for everything: what exactly they did, and what difference it made. Detail is what makes a thank-you land. And it doesn't have to be a long letter. Three honest lines, said to them, count.
screen: `THE GRATITUDE VISIT.` · `THE BIGGEST SHORT-TERM LIFT.` · `WE GUESS TOO LOW.` · `WHAT THEY DID, AND WHAT IT CHANGED.` · then, large: `SAY IT TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind, someone you've never properly thanked, and picture their face. In your head, shape three lines: what they did, what it changed for you, and what you want them to know now. Keep each one simple and true.
Epley. The researcher who found people guess too low about how much a thank-you letter will mean, a push to say it anyway. Today's word.
Your line: say it to them. Detail over drama: what they did, what it changed. That's day one hundred nineteen.

screen: `DAY 119 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: GRATITUDE WITHOUT THE FORCED SMILE.`

howItsDone: The gratitude visit, writing a letter to someone never properly thanked and reading it to them, is used in positive psychology courses and therapy, following Seligman and colleagues' 2005 study.

trapdoor: what you thought: saying thanks is just good manners.
what it means: a thank-you said to someone directly, with detail, which lifted happiness more than any other exercise in one early study.
what a scholar hears: Kumar and Epley, Psychological Science, 2018, found letter writers underestimate how surprised and pleased recipients will be.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'Think of' or tells the listener what they've felt; 'faded over the following month' corrected to 'held about a month, then faded' (Seligman 2005 reports effects lasting one month); Kumar and Epley named in the voice, 'surprises almost everyone', 'usually much more' and 'almost every culture' cut; the 'underestimate them' line clarified.
Seligman 2005 gratitude visit: confirm it produced the largest immediate positive change of the exercises tested and that effects faded within about a month.
Kumar and Epley 2018: confirm the finding (expressers underestimate recipients' positive feelings and overestimate awkwardness) and the citation.
Review cut 'Almost every culture has ways of saying thank you out loud' as an unsourced sweeping claim.
